The adjective seasonal means of, relating to, depending on, or varying with the seasons of the year.

To truly understand it, start with the word at its heart: season. A season is one of the four recurring periods of the year — spring, summer, autumn (fall), and winter — each with its own characteristic weather, temperature, daylight hours, and natural activity. The year moves through these four phases in a predictable cycle, year after year.

Now, when something is called seasonal, it means that thing is tied to that cycle in some meaningful way. It could mean the thing happens only during one particular season, it could mean the thing changes across the seasons, or it could mean the thing is shaped or influenced by whatever season is current.

1. Happening only at a particular time of year (not year-round)

This is the most common, everyday use. If something is seasonal, it doesn't happen all the time — it appears or occurs during a specific part of the year and is absent (or much reduced) the rest of the time.

  • Mangoes are a seasonal fruit — they're available in summer but not in winter.
  • In a beach town, the cafés and hotels are seasonal businesses — they're busy in summer but mostly shut in winter.
  • Flu is a seasonal illness — it spikes during the cold months and dies down in warmer months.
  • Christmas decorations in stores are seasonal — you see them in November and December, not in June.

The key idea here: availability or occurrence is limited to a window of the year.

2. Changing or varying according to the season

Here, the thing does exist year-round, but its quality, intensity, or character shifts depending on which season it is.

  • Seasonal temperatures — the temperature varies: hot in summer, cold in winter.
  • Seasonal rainfall patterns — some months bring heavy rain, others are dry.
  • A seasonal menu at a restaurant — the dishes change throughout the year to match what ingredients are fresh and available at that time.
  • Seasonal sales trends — a business may earn more in winter due to holidays and less in spring.

The key idea here: the thing doesn't disappear, but it fluctuates in a pattern that follows the seasons.

3. Done or needed at a particular season (recurring, cyclic work or activity)

This sense describes activities or jobs that are specifically associated with a time of year, often because that's when nature or demand requires them.

  • Seasonal workers are hired for a few months — farmers hire extra hands during harvest season, resorts hire staff in peak tourist season, and they're let go when the season ends.
  • Seasonal migration is when birds or animals travel to warmer climates every winter and return in spring — they do it every single year as the seasons turn.
  • Seasonal farming means certain crops are planted, grown, and harvested within specific seasonal windows.

The key idea here: the activity is periodic and tied to the natural or economic rhythm of the year.

The word seasonal implies a cycle — not just that something happens once, but that it recurs in a predictable, annual pattern. When you call something seasonal, you're saying it belongs to the rhythm of the year, not to a one-off event.

This is what separates seasonal from words like temporary or occasional:

  • Temporary just means something doesn't last — it has no implication of a yearly pattern.
  • Occasional means something happens sometimes, irregularly — again, no yearly cycle implied.
  • Seasonal specifically anchors the thing to the turning of the year.

If the monsoon comes every June in India, it's seasonal — not just temporary rain, but rain that is part of a repeating annual pattern.
Important Phrases and Compounds You'll Encounter

Seasonal produce / seasonal food — fruits, vegetables, or ingredients that are only grown and available fresh during certain months. Strawberries in summer, pumpkins in autumn, etc. Eating seasonally means eating what's naturally ripe right now.

Seasonal worker / seasonal employment — a job that only exists during a particular part of the year. Tour guides at a ski resort, lifeguards at a beach, harvest pickers on a farm — these are seasonal workers.

Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) — a real medical condition where a person's mood and mental health are affected by the changing of seasons, typically causing depression during darker winter months. The word "seasonal" here signals that the disorder's pattern follows the seasons.

Seasonal adjustment — used in economics and statistics. When analysts "seasonally adjust" figures (like unemployment numbers or retail sales), they remove the predictable ups and downs caused by the time of year, so they can see the true underlying trend. For example, toy sales always spike in December — a seasonal adjustment strips that predictable effect out to give a clearer picture.

Seasonal sale — a retail sale tied to the end of a season, when stores clear out their season-specific inventory (winter coats in February, summer clothes in August).

Seasonal greetings — a polite, general phrase used especially around the end of the year (Diwali, Christmas, New Year) that acknowledges "the season" without naming one specific holiday.

It's worth noting what the word doesn't mean:

  • It does not mean something is inferior or lesser — seasonal produce is often considered more desirable than out-of-season produce, because it's fresher and more natural.
  • It does not mean something happens every season — a seasonal fruit might appear only in one season per year, not all four.
  • It does not mean the same thing as "fashionable" or "trendy" — though people sometimes casually say "seasonal" to mean currently in style, that's informal and not the word's proper meaning.

If you had to condense everything to one sentence: Seasonal describes something that is connected to, dependent on, or varying with the natural cycle of the seasons — either appearing only during a particular time of year, or changing its character as the year progresses.

It's a word that ties things — weather, food, work, mood, business, nature — to the great repeating rhythm of the year. When you hear it, the first question to ask yourself is: In what way does this thing respond to or depend on the seasons? The answer to that question will always tell you exactly what "seasonal" means in that context.
